article_title: France Becomes First EU Country to Pass Law Banning Social Media for Under-15s
summary: Approved with one correction: the Australia fine comparison in the Analysis section cites a starting penalty figure (A$49.5 million) that is not stated anywhere in the cited Euronews source.

findings.message: Unsourced specific: Australia's original (pre-doubling) social media fine amount is not stated in the cited source.
findings.details: The Analysis section states Australia's under-16 ban was 'backed by fines that started at A$49.5 million and were doubled to A$99 million after regulators found compliance falling short, according to Euronews.' The cited Euronews snapshot (sources/2026-07/france-becomes-first-eu-country-to-pass-law-banning-social-media-for-under-15s/source-4.html.gz) confirms the doubled/new penalty is 'A$99 million (€63mn)' but never states the prior/original fine amount anywhere in the article (checked both the rendered text and the raw HTML/embedded JSON for '49.5', '49,5', and all 'million' mentions — none appear). The A$49.5 million figure is mathematically consistent with 'doubling to $99 million' (99/2=49.5) and is plausible as a real-world fact, but it is not verifiable from the source cited for it. This is a subordinate claim in the Analysis section, not the headline/summary/lead, and is being handled via a public corrections record rather than rejection.

content_preview.title: France Becomes First EU Country to Pass Law Banning Social Media for Under-15s
content_preview.summary: France's National Assembly and Senate approved a law blocking under-15s from social media, the first blanket ban of its kind in the EU.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

France's parliament voted on Tuesday to bar children under 15 from social media, making the country the first in the European Union to pass a blanket ban of its kind. The National Assembly approved the measure 279 votes to 81, according to [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/france-social-media-ban-under-15s-first-in-eu/), while the Senate backed it 243 to 2, according to [IAPP](https://iapp.org/news/a/france-becomes-first-eu-member-state-to-approve-childrens-social-media-ban).
...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis) at 729 words, within the 400-1200 word range for the News category. Clear, professional prose with no sensationalism. Both the government/child-safety framing and the civil-liberties/enforceability counterpoint (Big Brother Watch, Ines Legendre of e-Enfance) are represented, which is good practice for a policy story even though human_requested is false.
editor_notes.source_verification:
All 5 sources were read from the local gzipped snapshots in sources/2026-07/france-becomes-first-eu-country-to-pass-law-banning-social-media-for-under-15s/ (decompressed with gunzip and rendered to plain text for review) except PBS NewsHour, whose snapshot failed to capture real content (see below). Manifest checked first; all 5 manifest entries show status 200/202 with a non-null file and no error field, but source-2 (PBS) required special handling.

1. source-0.html.gz (CBS News, cbsnews.com/news/france-social-media-ban-under-15s-first-in-eu/) — 631KB real article HTML, read in full. Confirms: National Assembly-scale vote of '279 votes to 81' (article calls it simply 'parliament' rather than naming the National Assembly, but the figure matches); new accounts blocked 'from September' / existing accounts 'blocked from January 2027'; Macron quote 'France is leading the way in Europe when it comes to protecting our children and teenagers'; Big Brother Watch's Maya Thomas quoted verbatim on ID/biometric risk and on Australians 'bypassing age gates by drawing on fake moustaches'; von der Leyen quote 'It is clear we need age-appropriate restrictions to platforms' attributed 'last week'; Australia banned under-16s 'at the end of 2025' with '70% of parents polled...said their children remained on the platforms.' Does NOT contain the phrase 'a major step forward' (see finding below) or the words 'National Assembly'/'Senate'.

2. source-1.html.gz (Al Jazeera) — 189KB real article HTML, read in full. Confirms verbatim: Macron called the vote 'a major step forward' and added 'France is leading the way...'; Constitutional Council quote verbatim; Anne Le Hénanff quote 'If someone is under 15, the account will be closed' verbatim; new accounts 'blocked from creating new accounts from September 1'; existing accounts 'apply...from January 2027'; encyclopedia/educational exemption; Gaëlle Berbonde (52-year-old, Paris region) quoted on 'no other option' and separately on 'protect our children...from drinking alcohol' (matches submission's merged quote, corroborated as one continuous quote in the IAPP source, both derived from an AFP/AP wire piece — Al Jazeera's byline is 'By AFP and The Associated Press').

3. source-2.html.gz (PBS NewsHour) — SNAPSHOT FAILURE despite manifest showing file=source-2.html.gz, status_code=202, error=null. The decompressed content (1,998 bytes) is an AWS WAF 'challenge.js' bot-verification page with no article text at all (confirmed by reading the full decompressed HTML — it is a JS challenge shell, not the PBS page). This is a silent failure the automated fetcher did not flag as an error. Per review-submission Step 3b/3c, I treated this as a failed snapshot and fell back to a live WebFetch of https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/french-lawmakers-pass-sweeping-social-media-ban-for-children-under-15 (two targeted fetches). The live page confirmed: byline is Samuel Petrequin/AP (another wire-sourced republication); the France health-watchdog December report statistics ('90% of children aged 12-17 use smartphones daily,' '58% of them use their devices for social networks,' 'one in two teenagers spends between two and five hours a day on a smartphone'); the harmful-effects sentence ('reduced self-esteem and increased exposure to content associated with risky behaviors such as self-harm, drug use and suicide'); the Ines Legendre quote ('We'll also have to address the issue of existing accounts for those under 15. How do we identify them? How do we suspend them?' — submission truncates the source's longer quote but does not alter its meaning); and the Gaëlle Berbonde quote verbatim (matching Al Jazeera/IAPP). All PBS-attributed claims in the submission are confirmed by the live page. RECOMMENDATION: the fetcher/snapshot pipeline should treat AWS WAF challenge pages (recognizable by the 'awsWafCookieDomainList' / 'challenge.js' markers) as fetch failures rather than silently saving them as if they were successful 200/202 snapshots.

4. source-3.html.gz (IAPP) — 401KB real article HTML, read in full. This source directly and precisely confirms the vote counts under scrutiny: 'a 279-81 vote in National Assembly and 243-2 in the Senate' — both figures match the submission exactly, no transposition. Also confirms 'beginning 1 Sept' for new accounts and 'by 1 Jan. 2027' for existing accounts (matches submission's September 1 / January 2027 dates exactly); Macron 'leading the way in Europe' paraphrase; Anne Le Hénanff title and age-verification quote; Ines Legendre full quote (e-Enfance Legal Advisor); Gaëlle Berbonde full quote verbatim, explicitly sourced there to 'told The Associated Press' (confirms the AP-wire origin of this quote reused across CBS/Al Jazeera/PBS/IAPP).

5. source-4.html.gz (Euronews) — 425KB real article HTML, read in full (also grepped the raw HTML for '49.5', '49,5', and all 'million' occurrences). Confirms: Australia's ban 'became law on 10 December' with fines 'doubling the maximum penalty to 99 million Australian dollars (€63mn)'; eSafety found 'seven in 10' (70%) of children with accounts on the ban's start date 'remained active on Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok' three months later; the 10-platform list in the submission (Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, X, Kick, Reddit, Threads, Twitch) matches the union of the article's 'platforms...that do not take reasonable steps to comply' group and the 'remaining restricted platforms: X, Kick, Reddit, Threads and Twitch' group, with YouTube also named separately. Does NOT state the original/pre-doubling fine amount (A$49.5 million) anywhere — see finding.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: The two figures flagged for extra scrutiny in this review — the National Assembly (279-81) and Senate (243-2) vote tallies — are both confirmed precisely and identically by the IAPP source, with no transposition or rounding error. The September 1 (new accounts) and January 2027 (existing accounts) effective dates are confirmed precisely by both Al Jazeera and IAPP. The Australia A$99 million doubled-fine figure and the 70% non-compliance figure are both confirmed precisely by Euronews. The one figure that does NOT trace to its cited source is the A$49.5 million starting fine amount in the Analysis section — flagged as a finding and covered by a corrections record rather than blocking publication, since it is a single subordinate specific outside the headline/summary/lead and is mathematically consistent with the confirmed 'doubled to $99 million' fact.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. No editorializing, no AI self-reference, no loaded language. The 'What We Don't Know' section appropriately surfaces enforcement uncertainty and a civil-liberties counterpoint rather than presenting the ban uncritically.
editor_notes.originality: Checked src/content/articles/ for overlap. No existing article covers France's under-15 social media ban. Related-but-distinct prior coverage exists on UK Online Safety Act chatbot rules (2026-02) and the US Congress KIDS Act / California design code (2026-03), and a separate 2026-07-16 article on French antitrust action against Meta (different subject matter). This is a genuinely new story, not a duplicate.
concerns: The Analysis section's claim that Australia's fine 'started at A$49.5 million' before being 'doubled to A$99 million' is not confirmed by the cited Euronews source, which states only the new/doubled figure. Filed as a corrections record rather than a rejection since the rest of the paragraph (the A$99 million figure, the 70% figure, the platform list, the December 10 effective-date context) is fully confirmed and the flagged figure is a single subordinate specific, not part of the headline/summary/lead.

The PBS NewsHour snapshot silently captured an AWS WAF bot-challenge page instead of the article (manifest shows no error, status 202). This did not block review because a live WebFetch fallback confirmed every PBS-attributed claim, but the snapshot pipeline should be checked for silent WAF-challenge captures.
recommendations: File a corrections record for the unsourced A$49.5 million figure per Step 8.5/APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS process.

Consider a pipeline fix so fetches that return an AWS WAF/other bot-challenge shell (e.g. containing 'awsWafCookieDomainList' or similarly tiny content_length for a news article) are marked as errors in the manifest rather than recorded as clean 200/202 snapshots.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Strong, well-sourced News submission. Every direct quote checked was verbatim from its cited source (including two, the Berbonde and Legendre quotes, that trace back to a shared AP wire story republished across multiple cited outlets). The two vote tallies and the two account-transition dates called out for heightened scrutiny are all exactly correct. One subordinate specific (Australia's pre-doubling fine amount) is unsourced from its citation and is being handled via a public corrections record. Approved with corrections.
